Interview of Teddy Bunn
by
Chuck Rosenberg
Reel 1--Sides 1 & 2

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
P R O C E E D I N G S

I guess what I wanted to do was just today to talk about your early life, you know, like how you got started and everything. And then maybe get into some of the washboard stuff and the stuff with Duke. We'll cover that and then see how long that takes. So, could I just ask questions?
Could we do it that way?
Let me see, from the beginning, then, you were born in Freeport, right?
May the 7th, 1910. And your family had been living around there for a there?
Long Island, yeah. Rockville Center. Mother was born in Westbury, Long Island.
So your family had been there --
Do you know where they were from?
Let's see. Mother was born in Westbury, Long Island. My father was born in Hempstead.
You started playing guitar about nine years old, something like that?
I was playing guitar at seven.
What's your first memory of the guitar? Why the guitar? Why did you pick the guitar out?
Well, there was a piano in the house and a guitar and drums.
How come there was instruments around?
My parents liked to fool around with them.
And every time we tried to give a little
party at the house we all get these instruments together and tried to play them. So I took the guitar.
Yeah. The rest of them got the other stuff.
Was it hearing somebody else play the guitar that made you pick it, or --
No. I just picked it up.
You liked the sound of it?
I liked the sound of it.
That's why I stuck to it.
Could anybody in your family play very well?
My mother couldn't. My father played a mandolin.
My mother played a little bit of piano.
Christians, you know. They were Christians.
Did he play the mandolin in the
Yeah. Right. And they had a guitar, huh?
And they had a guitar and I picked up the guitar and I just taught myself. Wasn't so hard for me to play it either, because I just picked it up and started playing it, from hearing the music.
Yeah. I just found the notes, picked it up.
That's amazing. It's hard, you know -- did you have anybody, like uncles, come over and show you anything, or --
Well, I had my middle uncle, Chet.
His name was Chester. And we called him Uncle Chet, and he played violin.

And I mean he was a wonderful violinist. Chet Munn (PHONETIC). And I picked up the guitar and started playing, and they were surprised at me even trying to play, and what I could do to it when I picked it up. It was just a gift.
Huh. So did Chester play like with
Chey, yeah. He had a little group there. I forget the name of it now. It's been so long.
That must be about -- well, way back.
So he probably showed you a little bit how to hold it, or --
No, no. He didn't show me nothing. I just picked it up.
I saw. And how I went to the guitar like I did was that I seen somebody else, you know, just sitting down, trying to play whatever they picked up to play, and they had it across their lap, you know.
Strumming. And I just picked it up and started playing it, and they were surprised. Yeah.
And it didn't take me but a few days to get used to it. I guess that was the gift right there.
The ears. Because my son, like I remember when he first picked up my guitar -- well, I just actually had a little ukulele around.
And he held it just right. I mean he looked -- because kids have sharp eyes.
But his ear didn't tell him that much. His ear wasn't helping him out, you know.
But with you, it must have sounded like not only could you see what was happening, but you could hear what it should sound like.
Sure. Well, see, he's got a gift, and you keep following that up.
Oh, yeah. Well, he likes the drums.
For your own benefit and his too.
Yeah. When you first started playing, right, do you remember did you start performing a little later, like maybe when you were 15, 16, something like that?
Do you remember did you start per-
-forming, did you play in church, or -- No. I played in little dances they'd give, you know.
And then I'd get hired to play the little -- what do you call them now? I forget now what you call them. What do you call them things, now? See, that's been so long....
Social functions. And I just started playing and I was playing parties by myself.
My father would take me there and leave me.
And he'd come back at 12:00 o'clock and pick me up and take me home. And I made about $13, $14.00.
How old were you then, about, 15?
Oh, yeah? And then you just -- you
You got together with some friends then later?
No. I just kept it up by myself.
I was going to school, but I mean in the afternoons, when I'd come home, I'd get on that guitar. And everything I'd hear I'd play, try to play.
Before I finished I was playing it. Give me another cigarette.
Did you go into high school?
No? You just kept -- you just went -- when did you leave school?
I left school -- I got put out of school.
Yeah. I was a youngster, you know. Fighting. I had a fight with an Italian boy who used to try to whip me and take my marbles. Rocko.
Seems like there's a Rocko in every school.
How about that. Well, you can't blame them. After all, it's a free country, so they claim.
Yeah. So when did you first start playing like in a club or anything like that? Do you remember?
Well, I was playing for them little Saturday night functions, they called 'em.
I was playing in them when I was seven years old.
But then when did you make the change, you know, to more of a professional type of thing?
Yeah. Like a club, or something like that. When was your first club date?
My first club date was in -- let's see. Wow. First club date.
Must have been in the '20s, around '25, something like that?
In New York. Around Long Island, you know.
Of course that's still the same.
Was that with a washboard band?
I had my own group, yeah.
You were about 15 or 16 at that time.
Yes. And I took my own little group, and my mother would take me and leave me, and my father would come back and get me. And after that, I made about $7.00 or $8.00.
Were you the youngest in the group?
Yeah. Do you remember the late '20s, what you got involved in? You were talking about 1925, now.
There must have been a great improvement, like say between '25 and 1929. You must have --
So the transition from being a kid playing in Long Island to getting with Duke, you must have been playing all the time.
Yeah. I can't remember them now.
Yeah. Do you think that was when you got with, say, the Washboard Serenaders, or a couple of those washboard groups?
I was 14 when I got with a washboard group.
And we played in New York, at the Onyx Club.
And I used to make record dates, and they'd always come for me. They wanted me to play the guitar.
So, let's say we're talking about now maybe 1927, '28.
Somewhere in there. When did you first -- when were you contacted by the Ellington organization?
By Duke and that organization. Do you remember how that all came about, when you first worked
See? You know, these little places they'd come to after hours.
You understand? And I'd be playing in there and they'd come there and they'd hear me and they'd tell me where to come the next day if they liked what I was doing.

So I'd go to these different places that they'd invite me to, and Duke's band would be somewhere and I'd go there and sit in with Duke, because I was with Duke. Duke was giving me a little money, you know.
And every time I'd do that, I mean, I was known further, up and down the line.
Because in New York there's a lot of little [Ducks in demand] (Unintelligible) -- you know, little buildings.
You can go in and play after hours.
And I was there with Gladys Bentley. Do
She was a dancer and she had her own little place that she would be working in.
Gladys Bentley. And I'd go and play with her.
And she would sing and dance and you would accompany her?
And I finally got to myself thinking, you know, different things when you're young, that young people do, you'd go around, and I'd be hustling, you know, going out in the street playing guitar.
And I'd go and make me seven, $8.00 a night. Sometimes I'd come in with fourteen, $15.00. And I'd split it up with my family.
They'd give me a couple of dollars, to go ahead and do what I wanted to do with it.
You took it home to your parents at this point.

Yeah. My parents, yeah. And then I'd get up the next morning, and there'd be somebody out there in the middle of the street, coming to asking me do you want a gig? I'd say where? Well, they always could depend on me, that's one thing.
Yeah, I'd show up. So that's what kept on going until I came out here.
And your parents were supporting you, though.
They believed in what you were doing.
Yeah. Because I was bringing that money home and giving it to them. They knew what I could do.
When you were very little, even.
Because I never missed a night that I had
to work that I didn't get that money and take it home to them and they'd give me what they wanted to give me and keep the rest of it.
And take care of the house.
Right. So you were working with Gladys for awhile, and then you eventually got involved in playing in the Cotton Club with Duke?
And that was -- tell me a little -- can you --
I had a little group. Putney Dandridge was the piano player.
Uh-huh. He's dead, God bless him. And he played the piano. He and I worked there together at Duke's place when that speakeasy was going on.
Right. And you used to do duets, huh?
Sort of like -- did you ever hear of Leroy Carr and Scrapper Blackwell?
I think they were probably out of -- I forget where they worked out of. They might have worked out of Chicago or Memphis. I don't remember.
So you were doing the duets then.
And then was that part of the -- then when the Cotton Club -- they had big shows, didn't they?
They had about 14 girls dancing out there, you know, doing the show.
And I was up there and my little act would come on. Me and Putney Dandridge would get up there an do our little act.
Uh-huh. What type of material were you doing at that point?
Well, then, when did Duke ask you to actually play with the orchestra?
Huh? I kept it when I had that job that night.
They kept me there after I went over so nice.
But then, was Fred Guy playing also?
Fred Guy was drummer. I mean --
And then, so for awhile you and Fred Guy were both playing guitar.
At the same time. Is that right?
Not unless he sat in with me and I forgot that.
But I don't know -- Fred Guy was playing
Oh, I see. So Fred Guy was playing the rhythm banjo.
And you were taking the short -- the fills and the solos.
So did you make those recordings, the Victor recordings, before you went out on the road with Duke or after, do you remember?
Before you went out on the road.
So you really didn't know the book that well, did you?
It was all in my mind.
I knew I had to have this money, you know, and I just went on out and made it and brought it home to my
Uh-huh. So then, about that same time, about 1929, you went out for six months with them on the road.
Didn't you say that the other day?
Around -- some time after you made the records, "Haunted Nights," "Mississippi," and all those records, then you said you went out on the road for about five or six months with Duke.
I don't know. I can't think about it, that I did or not. I know --
You said Fred Guy got sick at one point.
I had to take his place for awhile.
You had to take his place.
And then you went our for awhile.
I went out with Duke, yeah.
And do you remember where you went? Was that New England tour, or where did you go, do you remember?
Buffalo. And -- boy, you're bringing it out now.
I'm going to give you no mercy.
We'll get the whole thing back.
Wow. Let's see. Now what did you ask me?
I just wanted to find out about going out on the road with Duke, if you went out for about five or six months.
No. Just a short trip, huh?
Uh-huh. You mean upstate and back --
Uh-huh. I see. And at that point -- you never have read music at all, right?
I wouldn't know what a note looked like. I know what they look like, but you know, I wouldn't --
When you played with the orchestra then, how did you know when to come in? Did Duke just point at you?
Did Duke just point at you and say --
During the rehearsal I knew where to come in.
Uh-huh. And you'd go through -- they would rehearse and he would say, 'Well, there's a spot here and --
After the trumpet solo, or whatever.
He'd look at me and that meant that that was my turn.
To come in there and fill in whatever it was, see.
What was he like to work for?
You mean loaded with money or loaded with the other stuff?
Well, he was making money, but yet and still, I never knew Duke to do nothing but take a few drinks.
He never used no dope as I know of.
Uh-huh. But he was a Scotch --
And he wouldn't drink too much of that. He just kept writing music.
That was his pastime, writing that music. And everything he wrote, I would be there to see where I came in it.
You'd really have to listen to it.
I'd just have to listen to it.

And he'd turn his head to me, you know, where I would come in at. And by me learning what they were playing, I learnt the whole arrangements, man. And I couldn't read a note, but I knew where I was supposed to come in and that's where I was.
He had no business telling me nothing because I knew it. All he had to do was turn his head off the piano.
That was my turn. Because he kept this up all the time.
That's right. Like Basie. You got that?
Did you have any friends in the orchestra. Were you tight with anybody in the orchestra?
Yeah, right. Do you remember any of that, personal friendships? Did you run with anybody?
No, I stayed to myself. I stayed to myself. That's right. I did stay to myself.
Because I couldn't learn nothing running around with them, because they was full of shit -- full of the devil.
They was full of -- running around.
Just picking up these women, you know.
I Cause But there was pretty women in that show.
I mean, all this -- that organization.
Them guys had a lot of women, boy. I remember that. One of them out of the show brought me to California.
You mean from -- when you came out, you mean?
And she got a job downtown, when the colored shows was in L.A.
She got a job there and stayed.
But she took care of me and when I went to -- where did -- let's see. Where's that President from?
Yeah. They took me to Georgia, in the same town he was in. I stayed there about a month.
Who took you there, the women from the --
One of the revues, yeah, a girl.
Before I came to California, yeah.
What were you doing in Plains for a month?
What were you doing in Plains? Hanging out, or --
Atlanta, or what town, do you remember?
It was a club in Atlanta.
Yeah. The club that I played at in a -- oh, boy, I ain't done this in so long. Boy. Atlanta, Georgia. That's when they -- [they've changed]prejudice yet, but they was awful prejudiced.
I was wondering what that was like, you know, 1940.
That was Atlanta, though, you were in.
Yeah. I come home on a boat.
Oh, you went down to Savannah --
Did you come through the Canal?
Teddy, how could you get from Savannah, Georgia to California in three days?
Yeah. Can you get there that fast?
Yeah. That's the way the boat came. Because I was on one of them tankers. I mean -- they carried them animals.
Cattle. I come home on one of them.
And all the way to the West Coast in three days?
Three days. 'Cause they Didn't lose no time.
Wow. Well, I guess with animals they've got to move them fast.
Well, anyway, we're getting a little ahead of the story, but that's really interesting. So you were playing
He stranded us down there and I had to get home some way, so I come home on a freighter.
And that's the only kind of money I had, to get a freighter.

Right. Well, I want to get back for a minute to the -- back around '29, you were with Ellington for about -- with the revue for awhile, and you were out playing around the area. When did you quit, or why did you separate from the Ellington organization? Did you have a better opportunity, or --
Yeah, now, let's see. Why did I quit from Duke? Oh, Duke was going on the road and he didn't have no use for no guitar.
See? He just had the big band. And he took the big band because they all read, see?
And whatever they put up in front of them they was cutting it out.
So the only time -- the reason why I left him, he asked me did I want to go, he asked me did I want to go.

And I told him no. I said, 'I don't think I can cut this.' So he said, 'Well, you think it over and if you want to go we'll take you.' So it come to it that Duke had to go right away, see, so he said, 'I can't wait no longer, Teddy. Do you think you can cut it?' I said, 'I don't think so, Duke.' So he said, 'I'll take the group on the road.' So he did.
So at that point he wanted you to read the charts. He wanted you to --
Yeah, he wanted me to read it, and I couldn't read it.
How come you -- I mean, did you feel at that point that maybe it would have been a good idea to -- would have been a good idea to learn, you know? Or did --
Well, I thought I should do the learning, but when I seen all them notes, boy, it scared me.
Did they have the guitar parts then, did they have the chords written out in notes, or did they have just the letter names?
They didn't have nothing down there for me at all.
Oh, so you had to learn --
I had to do it by ear. If I was going I had to do it by ear, because he didn't have the notes for no guitar, period.
Oh, so even if you could have read there was nothing for you to read.
Because nobody knew how to write for the guitar at that point.
That's right. I don't say Duke didn't know, because he could read period.
He could read fly skids, back-to-back.
Yeah. But there wasn't any charts.
But there wasn't no charts for me.
Fred Guy didn't have to read -- I mean he reads.
But what did he read? Did they have a banjo part?
Uh-huh. Just with the chords written down?
Uh-huh. So he had it easy in a way.
Yeah. He had it easier than I did.
But if you were going to have a chart it would probably have lines, single string stuff.
It must have been very exhausting to have to improvise with the orchestra. I mean, just make it up, you know.
Well, see, I've got a perfect ear, perfect pitch. And that's why I am so well know, because I've got perfect pitch. Anything I hear, I play.
And that's where my name went up.

Yeah. Well, maybe you thought that -- well, this is -- I'm not trying to make up the answer while I ask the question, but did you feel at that point that maybe there was other opportunities for you also, on your own?
Well, in a way I did.
In a way I did, but I didn't give no thought to only about makin' that bringing in money.
Yeah. So you weren't that ambitious, you were just like happy to be playing.
I was just glad I was gone.
See, figured that the trips he was supposed to be taking, and took, that I was so glad to be with him. So anything -- I just was a fill-in, understand, for what little parts that I had to play.
And I did remember them. And things that I didn't know -- I'd what do you call it?
Oh, I see. You'd make up --
In other words, I was a fill-in.
And Duke was crazy about that.
Well, some people, you know, think very highly of what you did, you know.
Well, everybody that was around said, 'My God, how do you do that?' I don't know. That's the answer for them right there, I don't know. How do you do it? I just hear it.
And I guess that's the gift.
So then, anyway, you stayed in New York and Duke went out on the road.
And was that about the time the Nephews formed up, or do you have your own group for awhile?
The piano player that you mentioned? Was he still with you? Putney.
Putney Dandridge, myself and -- let's see. Wow. Me, Putney and -- I had a little trio. There wasn't no bass in it at all.
Was it drums, then, or a singer, or what?
And Wilbur and Doug and all them is from St. Louis.
But you had a trio then.
For a couple of years there.
And that was playing at the Onyx or at the --
At the Onyx, huh? Was that about the time that you recorded with Spencer Williams?
When did the Spirits first form up? I guess they were the Nephews first, right?
Ben Burnie was a piano player.
I mean a leader. He was the leader of a band. Ben Burnie.
And the Sepia Nephews -- we were called the Sepia Nephews.
Uh-huh. And where was that? Was that at the Onyx, or was that somewhere else?
I don't know where he was playing then.
No, not in Harlem. It was very seldom that white bands came to Harlem.
Oh, Ben Burnie was a white band leader.
Uh-huh. So that was probably midtown somewhere, huh?
So he had a big show, then, an orchestra.
And then they used to feature the Nephews.
We used to be the Spirits of Rhythm.
But first it was the Sepia Nephews,
Then we turned around and got into -- what do you call it? Sepia Nephews, and then the other.
Yeah, the Five Spirits of Rhythm.
The Five Spirits of Rhythm, because that's when we added a couple of more on.
I see. Well, who was the original Nephews.
Right. So -- and not Doug's brother, though.
Buddy. Buddy. I took Buddy's place.
What the heck was Buddy's name? He was in --
He lived in -- Kansas City? No. Yeah, Kansas City. They're all out of Kansas City.
Uh-huh. So these guys were all coming into town to try and make it in New York at that time.
St. Louis. That's where they're from.
But they came to New York, right?
Yeah. We came -- let's see. They came to New York and I was in the Hickory House.
And they wanted you to take the place of Buddy.
So then it was like Ben Burnie's Sepia Nephews was -- it was Virgil Scoggins --
And you took Buddy Blurton's place.
So there was only four of you initially.
Yeah. Right. We changed it from three to four and two, you know, one.
And then how long did you play with Ben Byrne's show?
Uh-huh. And you were getting popular.
Yeah. In fact all of them was from St. Louis.
Oh, I see. Right. They didn't have a six string until they hired you.
No. When they got rid of Buddy I took it.
Because Buddy couldn't make it, you know.
And they was kind of fed up with Buddy anyway, because Buddy used to goof off, you know. To me he was an awful nice boy. Leroy?
What did you do with my cigarettes?
I was waiting till he gets through, because I don't want to interrupt the conversation.
Oh, that's okay. Let me turn it off for a second.
How much did that cost you?
Well, I rented it, you know.
Had to rent it for about $75.00.
Yeah. It's a nice machine. Anyway, that movie -- Mitzi somebody you think might have been in that?
Mitzi Mayfair, huh. With Ethel Waters and the Spirits.
Wasn't it one of these revue type movies, like Goldiggers or one of those movies, or did it have a plot or -- do you remember? Do you remember the film at all?
No? What did you sing in that picture? Was it --
The Spirits were in that one movie, right?
Well, Leo and -- yeah, was we on in that picture? Wow. You're going back, now.
"I'll Be Ready When the Great Day Comes"?
Did you do that in that picture?
I had a feeling that was the tune.

(Singing), "I'll be ready, I'll be ready, good Lord, yes, I'll be ready when the great day comes." "Didn't the good book say that Cain killed Abel? Yes, good Lord. Hit him in the head with the leg of a table. Yes, good Lord." I forget that other, now. " -- the sun refused to shine, but I'll be ready when the great day comes." Ain't that it?
yes, good Lord, I'll be ready when the great day comes." Wow.
I really like the breaks on that recording.
Some of those stop time breaks.
(Singing) "Didn't the good book say that Cain killed Abel? Yes, good Lord. Hit him in the head with the leg of a table. Yes, good Lord."
So you came out to California way back then. About '33?
But I mean, when you were on tour, were you here before then, on tour?
No. Yeah. Was I? Wait a minute, now.
Would you like to have a beer?
You're bringing up things now that I don't know. But you must be studying that book, whatever you've got.
Well, it's all, you know, bits and pieces.
But I've been trying to get a clear
Yeah. Well, I'd be glad to tell you if I knew. Because, you know, it's been so long.
Well, can you remember like some of the places that the Spirits played, you know? Besides New York, of course. But you must have gone out on the road with the Spirits, the original Spirits.
Yeah. Out here. We hit here after New York.
You didn't come out before then, then?
No, we come out -- I was through here, but didn't stop.
I see. When was -- you made the film, though.
Where did you make the film, then? Maybe the film was made back East.
Because they had movie studios back here for awhile, you know, in New Jersey, I think, in the '20s and the early '30s.
Wow. I didn't come out here with Ethel. I was back east with Ethel.
At the -- wait a minute, now. Boy, you brought up something then that's got me thinking. Somerset House? Oh, boy. Name the theaters in New York that's got these big shows come in.
Well, of course, the scene has changed so much, you know.
I mean, there was like the Pantages, the old East Coast, and the Palace, and some of those.
The Apollo goes all the way back.
No. Oh, we was in the Apollo.
Yeah. But this is really before my time, and a lot of these theaters have changed.
Was it on 52nd Street or more in the Broadway district, or --
Oh, out around 51st, 52nd Street, in West Philadelphia.
Like 52nd and Market, out around there? That area, 52nd and Walnut?
Yeah, that's what I'm talking about. That was out west of --
No, this was one on the main street, though. We was on the main --
I think that's been torn down. I think I know what you're talking about, around 51st or 52nd and Market.
Out there. Out past the arena, there's a big wrestling --
You know where they buy all this food?
On the main -- on one of them streets.
Not the Italian Market, but there was all different --
I don't think it's there anymore. That's all changed. Lancaster, Lancaster Avenue.
Oh, boy. You know where -- do you know where they've got that building in the middle of the street?
Well, you come down that street.
And at the end there's a little place you turn, and they served a lot of -- got food out there or something, a market out there. Mott Street, was it? No.
Mott Street. Mott Street. That's in -- no, that's in New York. That's Chinatown in New York, Mott Street.
There's a Mott Street in Philadelphia too, though. It's down in South Philly.
South Philly. That's where I was.
Oh, yeah. Because there was a lot of blues players back in South Philly.
You know, he was one of the originals, that guy.
I mean one of the early, really good blues players, like city blues players, from way back.
Right. Right. Him and who else was from Philly? Lonny Le Johnson --
Those were the big Philadelphia blues players.
And then people like Eddy Lang would learn from them.
As far as the blues style, you know.
Of course, Eddy Lang had his legitimate stuff together, too.
But the blues stuff, he used to work with those guys. South Street.
South Street is -- that's a funky place, man South Street is forever. South Street is forever.
But I don't know what exactly -- South Street. How about that.
South Street is all -- now is -- you've got the -- it's like a black neighborhood. And it's also like an area that's sort of like Greenwich Village.
Down around 4th and 5th Streets, near the river. That's right. There was a lot of those cats used to -- I think Bobby Leecan was from that area, himself.
I heard a recording of his recently.
But I heard an old recording of his,
Very advanced for that time, you know.
He's a light brown skinned boy.
Yeah, well, of course, I guess he's --
You didn't know him, did you?
Oh, yeah. Him and I had tests together about playing.
