And I told him no. I'm setting here ready for him to come, unnerved anyway, you know, because I knew I had to go out and do it, and this son of a bitch doesn't even come.
Yeah, I had that happen to me.
That's a hell of a feeling.
That happened to me once. In fact, you know, somebody I thought was a friend and --
-- you change your mind about it sometimes.
That's right. Wouldn't even let you know.

I had a whole thing. I had a whole set organized, we had rehearsed and everything. So I had this one set, and it was organized around him being a guest, you know, like guest star, I'd call him up from the audience.
We did quite a lot of rehearsal, made arrangements and everything. A big deal, right.

Half an hour before I was supposed to go over to play -- now, I put a lot of energy into that, you see. I played according to my own arrangements. He calls me up a half an hour before and said he's going for Washington, D. C. I'm in Philly, and he says, "Well, I've got this friend of mine, and blah, blah, blah, come down and play, and I said, "Well, are you getting paid for it?" and he says, "No, I'm getting paid tomorrow night and the next night, but tonight I want to come
down and learn the material." I said, "Man. Okay, we'll see you later. Later."
I don't want to take food out of anybody's mouth, you know, if something comes up.
Daddy, I don't have one. Unless you have some in your room.
Well, the only way you'll know is look.
So that's what I'm saying, boy. There ain't nothing. That's why I cut out of show business for awhile, you know, until I did get well.
To go out and take a whole lot more crap. I hope I don't have to do it.
Well, you don't feel that way about playing music. You're talking about a lot of the other stuff.
I know what you're talking about.
Because it's common sense, Chuck. Now, you go out there in the street knowing what you're going to do
that night, and go in there and here comes two or three musicians that's been playing with you -- is it lit, honey?
The other end. You've got it backwards. There you go.
And the best thing to do is don't go with them, so you won't get in no trouble like that. You understand what I mean, now?
Yeah, sure. they rip you off.
And once you find that out -- well, we've been talking a lot about pretty negative things, you know.
I'm just -- since we're talking about it we could turn it around and -- Talk about something else,
-- and talk about if there's any people you remember that you really enjoyed playing with, people that stand out, you know, in your memory, that everything was always cool, you know?
Well, to tell you the truth, the Ink Spots.
And little groups that I would get into around in here.
I wouldn't know the names of them now because they're out of mind, you know.
Yeah. Little things you'd be involved with --
Yeah. Since I stopped going into public life, which I think is best for me right now because I'd be in a whole lot of scrapes and be liable to get hurt because I can't see too much, you know.
Someone would come up to me and do something to me that I couldn't do nothing back to me, see, and that would worry me to death. They might as well kill me.
But I don't go out looking for trouble.
Nobody does, I guess. But they go out and get into it. Just by, you know, being whatever they think they can do.
Well, the idea of having your own place, you know, like a little restaurant or inn or something like that.
Where you could perform in your own place.
Yeah, well, that's wonderful. I had a little place in Palmdale.
Yeah, that's what we're looking forward to --
I think that would be perfect.
I had a place up there, and my goodness, that place was packed every night.
To the right, Teddy. No, to the right. Yeah. There you go. What's that, you say? You're talking about a place you used to have now?
You had a place up there before, then.
Uh-huh. Did you have a little bandstand set up and everything, or just like an area cleared?
Had a little place set in the back.
It was a nice place. It was a club. And I had the band in there every weekend. And I done good.
Why did you move away from there?

Well, I just didn't want to do anything. You know, some friends of mine got in some trouble up there. He killed a good friend of mine up there, and I just moved away from there because it got too hot for me. To tell you the truth. I didn't want to be around it. It was a very good friend of mine.
Just because they were people that
you knew, or -- Yeah. And he shot this man and killed him.
Were you a witness or something like that?
No, I wasn't no witness, but it was in my place.
Oh, yeah. It happened in your place.
So I just put it down. Then I got sick, too, you know, and that stopped me for real. So that's when things got a little boring. And then my sight left, gradually coming back.
But the way it seems now, I mean it's taking time. I can see you shaking your head over there a little bit.
I noticed when Tinker jumped on the chair over there across the room --
Could you see him, or was it more
No, I just knew where he was.
Is it quiet up there, the new place? Is it quiet so you can play?
I love to play music out in the desert, you know.
Because it's so quiet and everything. You can hear the notes.
It's real nice You can hear the music up there. It's real nice up there.
The notes kind of float out there.
Yeah, that's true. And you get more feeling. See, nobody's going to bother you.
The desert, you know, must have been really a new thing for you, you know. You came out here. You were from -- I mean there's no deserts in Long Island.
I know it. I lived at number 9 Nassau
Street in Rockville Center. Long Island. You know where Rockville Center is?
I've never been there, but approximately.
Yeah, right. It's sort of near Rockaway and --
Babylon. Bay Shore. Yeah, I was raised down there.
Was there much country there when you grew up?
Can I get you any more fruit juice?
I mean do you want some more fruit juice?

No? Okay. Let's wait then. It just popped into my head. What do you think -- we've been talking a lot about music and the life, you know, the life of a musician, whatever. What do you think is the most important thing to have together? You know, in terms of your attitude.

To be a musician, to function. You know, we talked a lot about different problems with leaders and middle men and, you know, incidents in the places you play, and all kinds of things like that. What kind of attitude do you have to have to deal with that?
You have to have a very nice attitude.
An understanding attitude. Because if you don't understand what's happening, you ain't going to make no musician, period.
And you won't. Because you're going to keep that on your mind all the time, till it's settled. And when it ain't settled, I mean it still goes on.
Have you heard from your wife yet?
Yeah. We were just talking this morning.
Yeah. I'll be going back in a few days.
And you take care of yourself when you do.
I'm going to fly back I think.
I will. I just hope I can get a seat for my guitar.
Sometimes you can sneak the guitar on the plane, you know.
You're supposed to pay half fare for it.
Here's the thing, see, if you put everything in -- you can check it as baggage.
And that doesn't cost anything extra.
But they'll mess it up. They won't take responsibility for it.
So what they've been telling people now is like, you know, buy a seat for it, you know, half fare.
Yeah. And then you take it on with you and you strap drop it in the seat next to you, you know. Well, that's fine, you know, if B.B. King, he can afford it. But I can't, you know.
But sometimes, if there's a lot of empty seats you can hand carry it on just like it was a bag, you know.
And just sweet talk the stewardess, you know.
And that's what I'm hoping to do.
Because that's the best way, because those bags --
Well, those baggage people will kill you, man.
They just throw that stuff around, you know.
And that's your livelihood they're throwing around. It pisses me off, I'll tell you. I had an argument with PSA last week, when I came back from San Jose.

Yeah, I flew back from San Jose. I took the train up. And they had this special service, right, where you're supposed to hand carry it -- they're supposed to -- you can't take it in the plane with you, but they'll hand carry it. In other words --
-- instead of on like the cart.
Yeah, but they'll take it by hand throwing instead of taking it on the cart, on the ramps, you know.

But they did that, loading it on, but loading it off they didn't notice -- they weren't looking at the tags. They hand carried the amp in, and the guitar come out on the damn conveyor belt, upside down, you know?
I'll tell you, I used to be a nice guy, man, but --
I'd love to be a bad guy.
I'm giving it up. I'm giving it up, man. I went in there and I screamed at those people.
I don't blame you. A thousand dollar instrument they're going to break up.
And they won't let you insure it anymore, see?
I used to be I'd insure it. You know, and at least you're covered then.
Now you can't even insure it. They've got you coming both ways.
Now, I think it varies from airline
to airline. But that's the trend, you know, what I was just saying.

Uh-huh. That's what they've got ahold of now, they're doing good business, you know. That's what they're doing. And everything they get on there, you know, as far as you're not carrying it yourself --
-- they'll take it themselves and do what they want to do with it. If it ain't insured, shame on you.
It's just like they don't want to be bothered, but the thing about it that gets to me is that I fly more than the normal person.
You know, it's part of the --
-- part of your profession, or whatever.
-- you're the public, a person that's going on the plane, and they're supposed to take care of your baggage.
Why don't you run the airlines?
Because you've got the right idea.
That's right. That's right. Drive me crazy.
But I guess you used to travel a lot by bus?
And Louis Jourdan. Did you fly with Louis Jourdan?
Yeah. Yeah, he never -- the only time we drove was when we were back east somewhere.
And we was in a hurry to get there, so we'd leave in a certain part of the night and by that next morning we'd be pulling in, 9:00, 10:00 o'clock in the morning.
We'd be pulling in. And we'd get a room.
Well, he you used to play pretty big rooms, right?
Like big rooms in major cities.
Not so much like staying in one area and working small rooms.
Louis got us That was good work. He's passed too, you know.
Dottie Smith. She lives in Philly.
Do you think she's back there now?
I imagine so. She got married.
You worked with a number of woman vocalists over the years.
Maybe you just did some recording with her.
"Yellow Dog Gal Blues," and stuff like that.
What do you remember about Haffa Brooks?
Well, Haffa married [out of the life,] you know. She married a nice looking white boy.

And he was a pimp. (Unintelligible). He beat her up, naturally, you know. Take her around to friends and someone else try to make her, you know. Because they seen him with her they tried to make her. She got home, she looked like Tack Annie, the way he'd swat her. And that kind of ruined her publicity. You don't want someone beat up going in doing a night's work. It's her own fault.
That's a shame. It is, you know.
You have to take responsibility for

your own life, you know. Well, she knew what she was getting into. Because she was told before she got married to him. And I can't understand why people want to act like that and making that money. I really don't. That's the secret, why? You know?
Why they have to act like that?
It must seem easier to some people, but --
Yeah, to someone that just wants to keep in trouble all the time.
But it doesn't seem to be that easy in the long run.

It's not. How the hell do you expect to succeed if you're going to go out there and spoil it before you get started? No way in the world, come up with that bad name. Well, I don't want to hire them because they fight, fight, they cause trouble. Any person that's got a nice place that wants to bring the group in, you know what I mean?
And they hear the publicity that's happening on the group.
And in case they want to make their money

too, you know, and you hire somebody that's -- 'No', don't hire them. It's a bad mark. And that's what's happened to a lot of musicians. More or less your race, my race, Chinamen, Japanese, any of them that go in with that shit, that's what's going to happen.
Yeah. They cause trouble for themselves.
That's right. A man comes all the way to New York. We was working at the Hickory House, the Spirits.
Working at the Hickory House. He come all the way from here to New York after this group, the Spirits of Rhythm, and brought us back here.

Had a bar and grill here in town, in California, in Hollywood. And the first thing they did when they got out here was get caught on account of a guy selling weed in the toilet. We bought weed and got locked up with it. Because the boy that worked in there was selling it. And we,
like a damn fool, bought it from him. He didn't do no time. We did the time. I done 45 days, and the rest of the boys done 45 days. For one joint.
A lot of states -- you know, nowadays a lot of states that's a misdemeanor.
In fact there's even a town, in Wisconsin I think, they made it into almost like a joke. It's a $5.00 fine.
Times -- you say time brings about a change.
It brought about a big change.
Some places, you've got to watch, like Texas. You can get in still pretty severe -- so it doesn't --
To even have a little roach.
Do you think some people play better when they're stoned? Or do you think it's like a fantasy?
It's a fantasy. Because you don't play no better. You think you do. You think you do. But you ain't
playing no better. Because when you ain't smoking and have to go on and do the same thing, you just put your heart and soul into it.

If you're a person that wants to make good. And I've always been the type, no matter how I felt I would be on stage when it was time for me to go on. I'd be all nervous before I go on, but when I got out there I done my work. And that's probably where I got the name from.
You used to smoke yourself, though, right?
No, I smoked pot anywhere I went. I knew I was going to be safe doing it.

Until I got busted. And then I quit. I said if this is what has to happen to me, and serve these 45 days for just a little cigarette I had, shame on them. And I quit. Especially when I started having my family, I said uh-uh. Nothing for me no more. Do you blame me?
It's like here comes trouble, you know?

Yeah. I thought I had got rid of one of the roaches I had in my pocket when the police took me in. I thought I had got rid of it in the place. And put my hand in my pocket and here was a little roach in my pocket. And what I done was just thrown it on the floor as I walked. And they was looking ahead so fast, following -- not following behind, because they had us by the arm, you know?
And I just dropped it. I don't know who found it, but I know I dropped what I had.
And this was here in Los Angeles. Boy, they used to be rough on you, they really did. I found out how rough they was and I quit, period.
Yeah. 45 days. Just on a little roach. Ain't that some shit? Cold, boy. Now I hear they're giving it out free, ain't they, some of it?
You never were drafted, were you, during the war?
Yeah, they called me, but I got out of it. I went down and took my test and everything else. That morning I had to go down to report, to get my suit on. I got a letter that morning. Rejection. So --
On what -- why were you rejected? Was it physical?
Was it a physical problem, or --
I don't know, to tell you the truth.
How did you feel about the war?
I felt like if I had to go I just had to go. I had no other way to think, to tell you the truth.
If it was me, I just had to go.
Uh-huh. You didn't have any -- did you have an opinion about the war itself?

No qualms at all. I just got rid of everything, what I had accumulated and got myself ready that morning and went on down there and they gave me something, and I passed the test, you know. [I passed it.]
So finally he told me I'd hear from them.
So I was rejected, [that was all I heard] That was it.
Uh-huh. I was talking to this one historian this summer who specializes in kind of black cultural history, you know?

And he's sort of putting together a theory that a lot of the bebop people, you know, in New York during the war, got into a lot of the drug use and acting crazy, you know, was actually something that they were working on that -- that was like something that they were doing on purpose, you know, to make themselves a little bit crazy, so they wouldn't get drafted. Because they felt that it was like, you know, white man's war, and why should they be bothered, you know?
Yeah, a lot of them felt that way. I know that.
Sort of like the Vietnam situation, you know.
And of course the problem when people make themselves crazy just so they can be crazy for a doctor in the Army is sometimes they go crazy, you know.
If you practice that for awhile, you know.
Yeah. And of course also a lot of them -- at least, you know, I've heard that since most of the Army camps, training camps, were down south --
-- a lot of the people from New York, you know, they didn't want to go down there for training or anything. They wouldn't have nothing to do with it, you know.
Yeah. Well, I didn't try to get rejected. I just knew I had to go, or else I wouldn't be worried like I was.
You know? Because I was worried why the devil they had to pick me. I went down there and took my test and everything else. Next few weeks they sent me a rejection.
Whatever they found out, I sure was happy whatever it was, but yet and still, I didn't have to go. But I was ready to go. Just like I said, time brought about a change.
Anybody in your group have to go in?
Anybody in your group have to go in?
No, the group -- I was working with -- with -- what's this bass player's name? The colored boy. What's his name? He's a big shot down in the union here in town.
Yeah. I went to work with Red Callender.
That was toward the end of the war?
I went to work with him.
Downtown here. In L.A. Yeah. You heard of Jimmy Bunn?
Yeah. I've never heard him play, but --
Yeah. He was just 50. You hit it. He's working up north.
Yeah. It was actually through his wife that I got your phone number originally.
Barney Kessel gave me Jimmy's number.
And then Jimmy wasn't home and I spoke to his wife.
Yeah. I saw them -- Skip -- no, Sharon showed me a picture.
Uh-huh. Yeah, Jimmy was on that heavy stuff. You didn't know that, did you?
He was on it. It took him a long time
to kick it, but he was on it. He kicked it --
Yeah. He was with me when he kicked it. Up in Frisco.

One of the things that we keep coming back to, you know, in the interview, talking and so forth, is how important family is to you. You know, like I think a lot of musicians that get into problems, maybe they have a problem with their family. They don't have it tight.
Well, I ain't had none. Thank God. Other than my boy. He's been a little trouble, you know. Naturally, kids --
It's not really anything that serious. But your parents must have been real close.
When you were growing up. Usually people that grow up in a family that's happy, you know --
They were. Only thing, they didn't get to see my children.
Yeah, it's a shame. My dad never got to see my kid, either.
But see, I took care of them. Still taking care of them.
I say I'm still taking care of them.

Yeah, right, right. That's what I thought you meant. I just wasn't sure. I think -- we're almost finished, really. Maybe just a few odds and ends, you know. Is there anybody that -- any musician that you can think of that you would have liked to play with but you never got a chance to? It's kind of a funny question, you know, because --
It's like there goes the bus I missed.
Well -- to tell you the truth, I don't know. Cab Calloway.
Uh-huh. You must have shared the bill with him at one time or another.
Did you ever share a bill with him?
No. Never got a chance to play with him either.
No. But I knew when he started.
You know, he always used to do that "Hidee, hideho," heidi, ho, you know, and all that.
And he stole that from us.
" Hi, hi, hi; hidee, hideho," heidi, heidi, ho. Now, we all done that down in New York. At an after hours club. That's where he stole that from.
But you still admire his music, though.
I admired him, yeah. I had nothing against him. We was making our money and he was making his.
Yeah. Well, you know, stealing is a funny thing, or borrowing, or whatever you want to call it. Some people are too stupid to recognize a good idea, you know.
Yeah. They don't know what to do with it,
in the first place, is the first thing.
So it's a compliment. That's right.
So he took it and he did something with it.
That's right. Sure. Heidi, heidi, ho. Hi, hi, hi. We had a song going in a club we worked in in New York.
(Singing) Hi, hi, hi; hidee, hideho. Heidi, heidi, ho. Hi, hi, hi. And he come in there one night and stole it. We didn't have it copyrighted, but what the hell could we have done with it?

So we didn't start to do any worrying about it. Probably could have if we went to court about it, you know, but we didn't. To each his own. We knew we started it, because we didn't hear it until we did start it.
So that's the only thing. Didn't worry me. Let him make his money. I was making mine. When you start bothering people about things like that, that's jealousy. And I don't go for that, jealousy. Why?
Well, some people feel that they only have so many ideas, you know, but only it seems like in your
career, like when I listen to the history of everything you recorded, that there was always a new idea coming up.
That's right. Why would I borrow someone else's idea?
Uh-huh. Or even one of your own.
One single. A little piece, you know.
That's right. Everybody's entitled to what they want to do.
Well, a lot of people don't have that confidence.
Some people think, well, they get an idea and then maybe another one won't come along.
Did you ever want to work with any of the swing, the larger orchestras?
I don't know. Charley Barnett, or Benny Goodman, or any of those. Did you have a desire to work with them, or were you more comfortable with the smaller groups?
Yeah. I was more comfortable, to tell you the truth, because -- there was one of the groups -- see,
Way down in the Village. Almost in the Village. It was in New York. But when he started rehearsing, you know, it was before he got the big band and going on the road, you know.
It was before Benny got to that. I just rehearsed. Mort Davis. You ever hear of him?
Well, Mort Davis had a club back east. In fact, it wasn't no club. It was just a place where musicians go in there and rehearse, you know?

Yeah. Rehearsal hall. And Benny was rehearsing in it, so I went in there one day. He listened and he started playing. So that was when Benny said, 'You want a job?' I said, 'Okay.' And that's all there was to it.
But did you work with him?
I done little things with him, that's all. Just making things. Mostly rehearsals. And the guy that had the place was named Mort Davis.
The rehearsal hall. Mort Davis. And from then on, I mean, I just said well, I might as well go on
by myself while the rest of these guys is making this money, I might as well go ahead and try to do it myself.

So I did. I'd go out to different clubs at night. I'd be beat, you know, but yet and still, I'd be making this money at night, and I fed my group for almost -- let's see -- about two months, I fed them.
Because the group didn't have any work?
That's right. It was bad in New York at that time. Harlem was nothing.
I see. Once the war came in.
Harlem kind of shut down, huh?
When the war came in, or right before the war?
let me think of a way to put this. It's a well known fact that musicians are attractive to women.
And women are attracted to musicians.
Yeah. And I was just wondering, like that creates different kinds of problems, you know. It can create family problems. It can create energy problems.
It creates jealousy. In the group. To tell you the truth.
You mean if one person has more women --
It creates jealousy in the group. So if you want to do anything like that it's the best thing to wait until you get off work.
And have your chick come to where you was living at. And that was the best, to keep down that aggravation and madness, evilness amongst each other, jealousy. You catch ?
It's bad, but that's the way it was.
Some people feel sort of like boxers,
you know, they feel they can only take so much of it.
It kind of wears people out.
That's just why me and Doug got into it that night. He was jealous because I was getting more attention. Jealous of me.

Because I was getting more attention. I was out there doing my act, throwing my guitar up in the air and bringing it back and playing, and he was just playing his tipple. I mean, shoot, he had no action, you know?
He was a nice looking boy. Light brown skin, nice hair, dressed nice.
Well, jealousy is a terrible thing, because --

It is. Especially in groups, professional jealousy. It's awful. I guess that's why I got out of it, too, to tell you the truth, because I didn't want to hurt nobody and I didn't want nobody to hurt me. That's the reason why I got out of it. And I was right. Instead of staying in a group, where arguments is going on all the time, everytime you do something that they think you shouldn't be doing, they want to fight and go on. I mean, shit, gee, get away from it. You wouldn't go up there and let a bee, if he stings

you one time, go up there and let him sting you again. If I had to be in a group like that, or any groups like that, I wouldn't -- I don't want to be around them. I'Cause that really goof's your mind up. (Unintelligible). I'm telling you.
I wanted to maybe end up with a comment, or we can maybe talk about this, that it seems like some of the traditional jazz performers are starting to get more popular again, you know.
There's a trend there, and it's a small trend maybe, compared to the type of stuff you see on television or whatever.
But nonetheless you do see people now, like George Barnes and Lionel Hampton, Stuff Smith, and oh, I could go on and on.
Is Stuff still living? Stuff's dead.
Oh, maybe I was thinking about Sugarcane Harris. Or one of those -- and Papa John Creech (PHONETIC).
Right. You know him from then?
Yeah. You know, these people are all making a fairly comfortable living now.
Uh-huh. Johnny Creech come out here and made a go of it. He really did.
Johnny Creech was crippled, you know.
He was, yeah. Lost his feelings and strength in his hands.
But he just got sick. He was a fiddle player.
Yeah, right. Where was he from?
I don't know. Never did know.
I don't know. And I guess you could find out by the one you went to the other day, (Unintelligible) where I was, down there.
He may have recorded for Cadet -- or, Modern Records.
Yeah, Jules has been very nice. He treated you nice, didn't he?
Well, he treated me nice personally. There wasn't any real business opportunities involved.
Yeah, sure he did. He's a decent guy.

He was a type. He was an alcoholic, boy. He was something else. As far as his clothes was concerned, he didn't care what you saw him in, to tell you the truth. He wouldn't press them and all, get them cleaned or nothing. I knew him. But he's been always nice to me. Anytime I call him and say, Jules, so and so and so, he says, Okay, Teddy, come on down here, you know.

I never borrowed no money from him. But yet and still I mean I wouldn't say I couldn't. Because I kept myself in the (unintelligible). If I needed it all I'd do is ask him and I know I'd get it. I knew his whole family.
It was the first thing, how he got in that business, through me.
Yeah. When I first knew Jules, Jules was doing nothing but going around, just catching acts, trying to catch acts.
You know. And then his brothers got in with him. And they started that thing they've got now. But it wasn't as big as they've got it now. They kept pushing. You know what I'm talking about.

They kept pushing and got together, and that's when they stuck together, the sisters, the brothers. No neighbors. He wouldn't want no neighbors in the business. Just that family. Jules Bihari. That's why it's called the Bihari Brothers.
Because that's what done it. And they
stuck together. Because Jules was a hell of a drinker. Jules used to drink. Every time you would see Jules he was drunk, and I mean drunk. So you know I must have known him a long time. That's right.
Did you know any of the other blues artists that he recorded in those days, like B.B. King, or -- did you ever meet any of those guys?
Yeah. I met him in Frisco.
And he was a kind of stuck up guy, you know. And I saw him back east somewhere. I've forgot the name of where I saw him, some town, back east, you know.
And he was playing one night dances, you know.
And as soon as I was recognizing him, he had a thing going.
Yeah, that's right. And he loved the blues. And if a cat loves the blues and can put his heart and
soul in the blues, good for him. Because that's where it is. And he got a good thing going on that blues, he kept it. He didn't try to invent something else. He kept it.

Oh, yeah, sure. I know his work quite well. What do you think that's all about? I mean, this is kind of a corny question, I guess, but what do you think the blues is really all about? I mean, what makes it so powerful?
In your work you take that blues and you put it into popular tunes and you put it into --
So it's kind of when the heart and mind come together.
I think of it as being shining or you know, -- brilliant can mean maybe kind of smart, but it kind of cuts through.

That's right. Just like you go play with a number somebody that's got a band, you know, and they'd say, "Oh, that's brilliant, that's brilliant, that's brilliant." That's something he had never heard before. You understand?
That's my idea of it. And he's smart. Because brilliant means smart, don't it?
Yeah, that's one of the things it means, yeah.
Yeah. Especially if the idea's coming out of that man's head, or whoever's head it's coming out of.
Yeah, right. Well, it's like the old cartoons with the light bulb, you know?
But except it's -- if you do it with music it's a light bulb that everybody can see by.
That's right. Once you put it out there ain't nothing happening. Is this thing going yet?
Yeah. I think that -- maybe that's --
-- that's about all. Is there anything you wanted to say or anything you wanted to wrap it up with?
Well, I think you're a wonderful person.
Well, thank you. This isn't about me, though.
No, but I still think you are a wonderful person and I'm doing all I can to help you.
Well, thank you very much, Teddy.

And for your own good you stick to it, because you can't lose. If that's what you want you cannot lose. And don't let nobody come in and jive you, "Well, Chuck, so and so is the case, so and so is the case." You've got your thing going, so keep it going, for your own good.
I appreciate that very much. I really do. And you know, it's a privilege to help --

And I can tell you come from a wonderful family, because you've been the same way ever since you come out here, ever since you and I met you've been the same attitude. You can't lose, long as you keep that attitude, and I doubt if you're going to change it now at your age.
No, I don't think I know how to.
There you go. Just trust in God, that's all, and that little fine baby you've got.
Where do you find God? I mean God
It can be a lot of different things for different people.

In my heart. That's the only place you can find Him, in your heart, because that's where he gets. Unless you want to change and get the devil in there, and that's when that devil does you in, don't he?

That devil gives you trouble. And as long as you follow him you'll keep trouble. And that's the thing to remember. If you've got him in you, change your ways, because you ain't going to get nowhere. That's what I found out until I got this family. Wasn't getting me nowhere.
So I changed. I had to change. That's even before I got sick. I had to change. And I believe in God. As long as you can think that way, you can't lose.
Okay. Well, thank you very much.

segments.chapter: Long Island boyhood
segments.title: Copyright notice, transcript header and interview opening
segments.summary: Archive copyright warning and Smithsonian header for the April 14, 1977 Rosenberg interview, then Rosenberg explains the plan to cover early life, the washboard bands and Duke.

segments.chapter: Long Island boyhood
segments.title: Birth and family roots on Long Island
segments.summary: Bunn was born May 7, 1910 in Freeport, Long Island; both parents' families were long-time Long Islanders.

segments.chapter: Long Island boyhood
segments.title: Taking up the guitar at seven
segments.summary: The house had a piano, guitar and drums; he picked up the guitar by ear and liked its sound.

segments.chapter: Long Island boyhood
segments.title: Uncle Chet the violinist and learning without teachers
segments.summary: His uncle Chet played violin in a family group, but Bunn learned only by watching and listening; Rosenberg compares his own son's first try at guitar.

segments.chapter: Long Island boyhood
segments.title: Playing parties and social functions as a small boy
segments.summary: He played dances and Saturday-night social functions alone, his father dropping him off and fetching him at midnight, earning about $13-14.

segments.chapter: Long Island boyhood
segments.title: Leaving school after a fight with Rocko
segments.summary: He practiced guitar after school, never went to high school and was put out for fighting an Italian boy named Rocko.

segments.chapter: Long Island boyhood
segments.title: First club date and his own group at eleven
segments.summary: His first club dates, around Long Island, came about 1925 with his own group when he was a child, his parents taking him to the jobs.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Washboard group at fourteen and record dates
segments.summary: Before Duke he played all kinds of groups, then a washboard band at the Onyx Club in New York, and was called for record dates.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: How the Ellington organization found him
segments.summary: Ellington's people heard him in after-hours places and told him where to come; he sat in with Duke's band and was paid a little.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Accompanying Gladys Bentley in Harlem
segments.summary: He played guitar for the singer-dancer Gladys Bentley at her own place in Harlem.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Hustling in the streets and giving the money to his parents
segments.summary: As a youth he played guitar in the street, brought home seven to fifteen dollars a night and split it with his family, who supported him.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Cotton Club revues and duets with Putney Dandridge
segments.summary: At Duke's Cotton Club he and pianist Putney Dandridge did a duet act between the revue numbers: blues, novelty tunes, ballads.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Staying on with Ellington; Fred Guy and the guitar role
segments.summary: Duke kept him after his first night; Fred Guy played rhythm banjo while Bunn took fills and solos.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Victor recordings made before going on the road
segments.summary: He made the Victor records before touring with Duke, not knowing the book and winging it from his ear.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: A short road trip with Ellington
segments.summary: When Fred Guy got sick Bunn filled in and went out with Duke upstate and around Connecticut for a short time, not five or six months.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Never reading music; how he knew his cues in the orchestra
segments.summary: He never read notes and learned his place at rehearsal; Duke would look at him when it was his turn to fill in.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: What Duke Ellington was like to work for
segments.summary: Duke was fine, took a few drinks, used no dope, and kept writing music; Bunn learned the arrangements by ear.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Keeping to himself among the Ellington musicians
segments.summary: He avoided running around with the band, who chased women, and recalls the pretty women in the show.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: A revue girl takes him to Georgia in 1940
segments.summary: One of the Cotton Club-type revue girls took care of him and took him to Plains, Georgia for about a month before he came to California.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Playing in Atlanta in 1940 and Southern prejudice
segments.summary: He was playing at a club in Atlanta and says the South was awfully prejudiced then.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Stranded in Georgia and coming home on a cattle freighter
segments.summary: Stepin Fetchit stranded the group; Bunn got home through the Panama Canal on a cattle freighter in three days.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Why he left Ellington: he could not read the charts
segments.summary: Duke took the big band on the road and offered to take Bunn if he could read, but the notes scared him so he stayed.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: No guitar parts existed; how Fred Guy read
segments.summary: There were no guitar charts for him, so he had to play by ear, while Fred Guy read chord charts on banjo.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Perfect pitch and being a fill-in man
segments.summary: He credits his perfect pitch for his reputation and says he filled in what he did not know, which Duke liked.

segments.chapter: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
segments.title: Trio with Putney Dandridge at the Onyx and the Spencer Williams recording
segments.summary: After Duke left he led a trio with Putney Dandridge at the Onyx, around the time he recorded with Spencer Williams.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Ben Bernie's Sepia Nephews becomes the Spirits of Rhythm
segments.summary: The group started as Ben Bernie's Sepia Nephews in a midtown theater show, later billed as the Spirits of Rhythm and the Five Spirits of Rhythm.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Original members and replacing Buddy Blurton
segments.summary: The original Nephews were Leo Watson, Doug Daniels, Virgil Scoggins and Buddy Blurton, all from St. Louis; Bunn took tiple player Buddy's place and stayed with Bernie about six months.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Interruption: cigarettes and the rented recorder
segments.summary: Household talk interrupts, and Rosenberg says he rented the machine for about $75 a month.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: The Ethel Waters film and "I'll Be Ready When the Great Day Comes"
segments.summary: They discuss a revue-type movie with Ethel Waters and the Spirits, and Bunn sings the Spirits' tune from it.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: When the Spirits first reached California; where the film was made
segments.summary: Bunn says he came west in 1940, passed through earlier without stopping, and worked with Ethel Waters back east.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Theaters in Philadelphia and the Apollo
segments.summary: Trying to place a theater in the colored neighborhood of Philadelphia where the Spirits played, they settle on South Philly.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Philadelphia blues guitarists: Bobby Leecan and Lonnie Johnson
segments.summary: Rosenberg names early Philly blues guitarists; Bunn knew Bobby Leecan and says they had playing contests which he always won.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Meeting Eddie Lang through Paul Whiteman
segments.summary: Bunn met guitarist Eddie Lang in New York years ago, when Lang was with Paul Whiteman.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Collectors, old records and the Bihari brothers' studio
segments.summary: They talk about collectors holding old Lang recordings, and Bunn says he made many records for Jules Bihari's small studio in Glendale.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Hawaiian guitarists and Roy Smeck
segments.summary: Bunn never played in the big white shows with Hawaiian guitarists like Roy Smeck; old recordings bring back memories.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: How the Spirits picked up tunes from audiences
segments.summary: The Spirits learned whatever the audience requested or they heard, being good enough to pick up tunes quickly.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Booking by Nat Nazzara and the Spirits' tour cities
segments.summary: Nat Nazzara booked the Spirits at the Onyx home base and to Philadelphia, Boston and Washington but not Baltimore or New Jersey.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Playing the Howard Theater in Washington
segments.summary: The Spirits played the colored Howard Theater in Washington and Bunn also played the Apollo.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Stranded in Florida and driving home in a 1927 Cadillac
segments.summary: After Ben Bernie and Stepin Fetchit fought over money in Miami, Bunn bought a 1927 Cadillac for $300 and drove everyone home.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: The guitar in the 1930s; playing at the mike with Ellington
segments.summary: Guitar and tiple groups were unusual, banjo was fading, and with Duke he held the guitar up near the microphone.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Feeding the broke band; pot smoking and the fight with Doug
segments.summary: Bunn passed the hat to feed the band, who smoked pot all night, and he split Doug's tiple in a fight in Buffalo.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Acting like a father to the young Spirits
segments.summary: He was unmarried then and tried to be nice to the 19- and 20-year-old members.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Why he stayed with the Spirits and then left after the Buffalo fight
segments.summary: Bookings and a pact to stick together kept him until the fighting and the Buffalo clash with Doug made him quit.

segments.chapter: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
segments.title: Freelancing and record dates before California
segments.summary: After leaving he freelanced, made records with Jimmy Noone, Frankie Newton and John Kirby's group.

segments.chapter: Moving to California and the war years
segments.title: Deciding to go to the Coast in 1940
segments.summary: He had long wanted to go to California, quit the Spirits, played in Atlanta and took the $40 freighter to San Pedro.

segments.chapter: Moving to California and the war years
segments.title: Arriving in California cold and passing the hat
segments.summary: He knew no one in California and survived passing the hat for 25 to 40 dollars a night.

segments.chapter: Moving to California and the war years
segments.title: Bringing the Spirits out to California by car
segments.summary: He returned east, found the Spirits in Philadelphia with the Whitman Sisters, and drove west with Leo, Doug, Wilbur and others.

segments.chapter: Moving to California and the war years
segments.title: Arrested for marijuana in Los Angeles
segments.summary: He was jailed 45 days in the L.A. County Jail for a joint and swore off pot afterwards.

segments.chapter: Moving to California and the war years
segments.title: The group breaks up and the draft board turns him away
segments.summary: The Spirits broke up out west, and the Army gave him an induction physical but never inducted him.

segments.chapter: Moving to California and the war years
segments.title: Adapting to the new sounds with single-string playing
segments.summary: He adapted to changing music by ear, ignoring complex chords and playing single string.

segments.chapter: Moving to California and the war years
segments.title: Young West Coast players; Nat Cole and Oscar Moore
segments.summary: On arrival in L.A., Nat Cole's group was the goal; Oscar Moore was a fine guitarist but jealous of Bunn.

segments.chapter: Moving to California and the war years
segments.title: Leading the Teddy Bunn Group; Leonard Feather
segments.summary: During the war years he had his own group, and Leonard Feather looked him up for pickup record dates.

segments.chapter: Moving to California and the war years
segments.title: The decline and death of Leo Watson
segments.summary: After the Spirits broke up around 1943 Leo drank wine downtown and died there, though he recorded with Vic Dickenson and Artie Shaw.

segments.chapter: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
segments.title: Listening to Leo Watson's last recordings
segments.summary: They play Leo's records ("Sunny Boy", "Jingle Bells"), and Bunn laments that Leo died young and should have been a millionaire.

segments.chapter: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
segments.title: Leo Watson's scat singing and why no one matched it
segments.summary: Leo started with background fills and grew into original scat solos; Bunn has heard nobody like him, and Eddie Jefferson also called him the greatest.

segments.chapter: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
segments.title: Leo's character, drinking and clothes
segments.summary: Leo had a good attitude but drank heavily after reaching California, slept in Bunn's house with melting ice cream, and loved dressing well.

segments.chapter: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
segments.title: Tommy Ladnier and the Panassie session personnel
segments.summary: Rosenberg introduces the 1938 Panassie session with Ladnier, Mezzrow, Pops Foster and Manzie Johnson; Bunn remembers Ladnier as a wonderful man and musician.

segments.chapter: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
segments.title: Mezz Mezzrow as leader and his habits
segments.summary: Mezzrow called the session; Bunn got along with him but disliked his pot habit, which made Mezz sloppy and unreliable.

segments.chapter: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
segments.title: Working with Pops Foster and Manzie Johnson
segments.summary: Bunn played with Pops Foster four or five times and found him solid; he knew little about Manzie Johnson beyond being a good musician.

segments.chapter: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
segments.title: What he recalls of the Panassie session and meeting Hugues Panassie
segments.summary: He cannot remember the day or tunes, but players were often up all night before record dates; Panassie was wonderful to him.

segments.chapter: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
segments.title: Kicking off tunes and keeping the hungover players straight
segments.summary: The others depended on Bunn to start the tunes; he was tired of being called to keep things straight, and he cannot recall where "If You See Me Coming" came from.

segments.chapter: Leo Watson and the Panassie sessions
segments.title: Sidney Bechet, Blue Note sessions and how sessions ran
segments.summary: Bunn knew Bechet through Mezz and did Blue Note sessions with him; sessions ran with a standard repertoire, natural rehearsal and pointing for solos.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: Tuning down a half tone and the heavy-gauge strings
segments.summary: He tuned his guitar down a half step with medium strings, giving a fat sound while still allowing bends.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: His guitars: Stella, Martin and the Epiphone
segments.summary: Rosenberg traces photos of round-hole flat-top guitars to the arch-top Epiphone; Bunn says he played whichever guitar sounded best.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: Fingering and picking technique
segments.summary: He played with first two fingers alternating and the thumb on bass strings, and did glisses with thumb or the whole hand.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: The Blue Note solo records, "Blues Without Words" and "King Porter Stomp"
segments.summary: He was told to play whatever he liked, hummed on the first, wailed on "King Porter Stomp", and was paid only for the sessions.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: Floating over the beat unlike Eddie Lang
segments.summary: Rosenberg says his playing stood out for floating away from the beat and returning, unlike Eddie Lang; Bunn says that is how his mind went.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: What went through his mind when soloing
segments.summary: Bunn does not know how he thought when soloing; he says the secret is the ear, not reading notes.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: The guitar's status in the 1930s and forgotten musicians
segments.summary: He says the guitarist who played best got the work, and laments that good musicians go unheard, himself sidelined by illness.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: Adapting to the times and ambition (Irving Ashby)
segments.summary: Some players adapt to new tunes and some lack ambition or have enough money; Bunn still wanted to keep working.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: Taking rhythm and blues jobs in the 1950s as just work
segments.summary: He worked with r&b groups and singers like Hadda Brooks as a job for pay, recalling how as a boy he gave party money to his parents.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: Where he lived in New York in the 1930s
segments.summary: He lived with his folks on Long Island, then uptown and in Harlem, passing the hat for 15 to 40 dollars.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: Fishing and horses
segments.summary: Rosenberg asks if he fished back then; Bunn says no, though he sees fishing as a good way to occupy the mind.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: Flying to Bermuda with Louis Jordan's group
segments.summary: His first flight took him to Bermuda for about a month with Louis Jordan and Charlie Gray, playing electric guitar.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: Honolulu with Jack McVey at Don the Beachcomber's
segments.summary: He went to Honolulu with Jack McVey's show band, with Louise Beavers singing and a rhythm and blues repertoire.

segments.chapter: Guitar technique and later career
segments.title: Reel 2 header and sound check (April 29, 1977)
segments.summary: Second session begins in Washington with a microphone test and chatter about the day.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Listening to Jim Hall's trio
segments.summary: They listen to a live Jim Hall trio recording of "Scrapple from the Apple" and Rosenberg asks Bunn to repeat his comments.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Bebop as changes without melody; Dizzy Gillespie
segments.summary: Bunn calls bop musicians' music with weird notes and no melody, started by Dizzy Gillespie and copied by everyone.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Keeping up with trends and building a tune from the strain
segments.summary: Changing with trends takes study and a working mind, and he describes putting in notes that fit each strain he hears.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: "Jackson's Nook" and bop-flavored blues with Pony Poindexter
segments.summary: He recorded "Jackson's Nook" in San Francisco at a club owned by a Jackson, and says he had to keep up with the times.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Feeling in the melody and knowing the instrument
segments.summary: He says feeling is in the melody and as long as you know it you can go anywhere with it, the music coming automatically if you know your instrument.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Rhythm and blues sessions versus Bechet and Jelly Roll dates
segments.summary: Asked whether 1950s r&b work felt like baby music, Bunn says he did his best and was simply paid for it.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Royalties, selling tunes outright and not worrying about the business
segments.summary: He got small royalties from "I've Come a Long Ways, Baby", sold tunes to publishers for a flat fee, and just wanted his check.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Which groups he enjoyed most and the Ink Spots
segments.summary: The Spirits were his favorite; Louis Jordan, Ink Spots, Edgar Hayes and others were jobs, and he never recorded with the Ink Spots.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: King Oliver
segments.summary: Bunn heard Joe Oliver play but did not sit in with his groups.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Recording with Jimmy Noone in Chicago
segments.summary: The Noone records were made in Chicago; Noone played clarinet and soprano sax.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Drinking and nerves among performers; Leo throws things from the window
segments.summary: Bunn says performers drank to face the stage, with stage fright; Leo got drunk on gin and threw things out a seventh-floor window.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Radio broadcasts on WINS
segments.summary: Rosenberg wants to look for transcriptions of Bunn's WINS broadcasts in New York.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Pianist Bob Laine and Nick's in the Village
segments.summary: He worked a long time with Swedish pianist Bob Laine at Nick's in Greenwich Village.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: The unreleased Adrian Rollini trio record
segments.summary: He recorded for anyone he could make a dollar with, including a Brunswick trio session under Adrian Rollini's name.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Hot Lips Page trio records and "Evil Man's Blues"
segments.summary: Bunn recorded the Hot Lips Page trio with Wellman Braud and sang the vocal; he never interfered with other people's sessions.

segments.chapter: Bebop, business and recordings
segments.title: Intros, lead melody and bass figures on the Page session
segments.summary: He explains kicking off tunes because he could play the melody, his many intro ideas and bass figures, and a Roy Rogers sideman who may have copied him.

segments.chapter: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
segments.title: Bubber Miley at the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Bunn remembers Bubber Miley as an alcoholic who could read everything Duke wrote; they worked the Cotton Club together.

segments.chapter: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
segments.title: What Duke Ellington was really like
segments.summary: Bunn found Duke a nice, alert businessman with common sense who kept people at a distance.

segments.chapter: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
segments.title: Guitarists in New York: Eddie Lang compared
segments.summary: There were few single-string guitarists in New York; he heard Eddie Lang with Crosby and Whiteman and says Lang lacked ideas.

segments.chapter: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
segments.title: Al Casey and knowing the ropes
segments.summary: He did not think much of Al Casey, who knew chords but not enough.

segments.chapter: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
segments.title: Keeping up with the trend and professional jealousy
segments.summary: He says he kept pushing from Duke on, while other musicians get jealous and overwhelmed by what they cannot do.

segments.chapter: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
segments.title: Jealousy with Doug Daniels and the pot-rolling nights with Leo
segments.summary: Doug Daniels would not share solos with Bunn's six strings, and he and Leo rolled pot all night.

segments.chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
segments.title: Recording with Lionel Hampton: "Charlie Was a Sailor"
segments.summary: They listen to the Victor session with Lionel Hampton, made out west around 1940 on a tour with a four-piece combo.

segments.chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
segments.title: Playing his first electric guitar, a Gretsch
segments.summary: He bought a cheap Gretsch electric and describes playing lighter, sustained notes and no feedback problems.

segments.chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
segments.title: Keeping the guitar heard in Hampton's small group
segments.summary: Against vibes and piano in Hampton's quartet he used higher notes to be heard.

segments.chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
segments.title: Blistered fingers and punishing show schedules with the Spirits
segments.summary: He bore down so hard he got blisters in the 1930s, and the Spirits sometimes did up to seven shows a day; he always arrived tuned.

segments.chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
segments.title: Why he tuned down: blending with Doug Daniels's tiple
segments.summary: He began tuning lower to blend with the high tiples, especially Doug's, and debates with Rosenberg whether it was half or whole step.

segments.chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
segments.title: Being dependable and always getting paid
segments.summary: He says he was known because he never disappointed anyone, always arrived early and expected his money right after the job.

segments.chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
segments.title: "Wearyland Blues" with J.C. Higginbotham and how he held notes
segments.summary: They play the Blue Note record with Higginbotham and Albert Ammons from the mid-1930s; Bunn can only credit his ear and a gift for his held notes.

segments.chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
segments.title: Working with piano players; no strap; Meade Lux Lewis
segments.summary: Rosenberg says Bunn's single-string style suits pianists; Bunn knew where the four beats were, and held the guitar with his elbow and no strap.

segments.chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
segments.title: Frankie Newton sessions and leaving New York for California
segments.summary: He did several sessions with Frankie Newton and left New York after family friction, on an offer from the Hickory House.

segments.chapter: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
segments.title: Smog in Palmdale and bassist Oscar Pettiford
segments.summary: Talk of airplanes and smog in Palmdale brings up Oscar Pettiford, who worked with Bunn and drove through the fog.

segments.chapter: Noone, Kirby and family
segments.title: Jimmy Noone Orchestra on Decca; Noone's background
segments.summary: They play Noone records, and Bunn says Noone was a New Orleans musician whose smooth style sounded like clarinet study.

segments.chapter: Noone, Kirby and family
segments.title: John Kirby's group and a fight with its guitarist
segments.summary: John Kirby formed his group himself; Bunn recalls hitting its jealous guitarist with his guitar after wisecracks about his solos.

segments.chapter: Noone, Kirby and family
segments.title: Red McKenzie's prejudice
segments.summary: Bunn says Red McKenzie was prejudiced although he used the Spirits for his sessions, as is true of St. Louis generally.

segments.chapter: Noone, Kirby and family
segments.title: Where the name Spirits of Rhythm came from
segments.summary: The members were from St. Louis; under Ben Bernie they were the Sepia Nephews and then took the Spirits of Rhythm name.

segments.chapter: Noone, Kirby and family
segments.title: His parents, brothers and the family quarrel that sent him west
segments.summary: His father was Everett Arlington Bunn, mother Elizabeth Jackson, brothers Roger and Kenneth; Kenneth's drunken cursing at their mother made him leave.

segments.chapter: Noone, Kirby and family
segments.title: Deep-sea fishing and Tal Farlow
segments.summary: He fished off San Pedro to relax, and they talk of guitarist Tal Farlow, a fisherman and sign painter.

segments.chapter: Noone, Kirby and family
segments.title: Hustling clubs for sets; Bob Landon in Palm Springs
segments.summary: He went from club to club to sit in and make money, and mentions pianist Bob Landon, who played with him at Nick's and now lives in Palm Springs.

segments.chapter: Noone, Kirby and family
segments.title: Johnny Dodds and the Kirby guitarist battle
segments.summary: Dodds said nothing against Bunn; the hassle was with a guitarist in John Kirby's group at the Onyx.

segments.chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
segments.title: Reel 2 side 2 header (April 28, 1977)
segments.summary: Transcript header for the next session in Washington.

segments.chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
segments.title: Louis Jordan's band and its influence
segments.summary: Bunn describes Jordan's Philadelphia group (Mobley, Rice, Gray, Dottie Smith), the rhythm and blues feel, and says they only played one-nighters and never recorded.

segments.chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
segments.title: Joining Louis Jordan in Las Vegas and the Bermuda trip
segments.summary: Bunn worked about two years with Jordan after the war, joining him in Las Vegas from a lounge group.

segments.chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
segments.title: Working with Charlie Gray's Ink Spots and Deek Watson
segments.summary: He freelanced with Charlie Gray's Ink Spots and Deek Watson, noting Gray was egotistical and paid the band last, then drifts to friends in Seattle.

segments.chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
segments.title: Musicians' union Local 802 and how it helps
segments.summary: He joined 802 with Duke around 1929, rejoined after 1970, and says the union finds work according to reputation.

segments.chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
segments.title: Lathing with his father between music jobs
segments.summary: He did house lathing with his dad and brother when music work got lean, using a hatchet and nailing fast.

segments.chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
segments.title: Day jobs: cooking and bartending
segments.summary: Rosenberg talks about his own short-order cook and bartending jobs.

segments.chapter: Louis Jordan, Ink Spots and the union
segments.title: Whether the musicians' union gets players full-time work
segments.summary: Most union members do not live off music, so players take any gig; Bunn says he would be working if he were not sick.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Edgar Hayes and the hundred-dollar bill in San Francisco
segments.summary: With Edgar Hayes's Riverside-era group, a woman tipped Bunn a hundred dollars on the bandstand, Hayes tried to take it and Bunn hit him, then Hayes cut his finger at his door.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Bunn's philosophy as a bandleader: equal shares and fines
segments.summary: As a leader he split pay equally, fined latecomers into a trust fund, and contrasts Edgar Hayes wanting everything.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Never speaking to Edgar Hayes again
segments.summary: Rosenberg once phoned Hayes's house looking for Bunn; Bunn says he never dealt with Hayes after the fight.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Listening to current music and electronic guitar effects
segments.summary: He listens mainly to keep his mind ahead, and says he could use any effect depending on whether it feels right.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: "It's all in your mind": attitudes and why people act as they do
segments.summary: Bunn muses that whatever people do is in their minds, including why people want to hit others or why interviewer and interviewee are together.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Friends who let him down and why he left show business for a while
segments.summary: A friend never came to take him to a parade gig; both men trade stories of disappointment, and he left public life until well.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Favorite groups: Ink Spots and Lionel Hampton; avoiding public life
segments.summary: He most enjoyed the Ink Spots and Lionel's group, and stays out of public life because he cannot see well.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Bunny's Barbecue in Palmdale and his sickness
segments.summary: He ran a club called Bunny's Barbecue in Palmdale and Las Vegas, left after a friend was shot in it, then fell ill and lost sight.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Playing music in the desert; growing up in Rockville Center
segments.summary: The quiet desert suits playing, and he recalls growing up at 9 Nassau Street, Rockville Center, Long Island, amid woods.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: The attitude a musician must have
segments.summary: He says a musician needs an understanding attitude or problems stay on the mind.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Talk about Rosenberg's family and flying with a guitar
segments.summary: Rosenberg talks about flying home and airlines mishandling guitars, with Bunn commiserating.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Flying with the Ink Spots and Louis Jordan; Dottie Smith
segments.summary: They flew or took trains, driving only when in a hurry; Jordan got good work and Dottie Smith settled in Philadelphia.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Hadda Brooks and the toll of bad behavior
segments.summary: Bunn says Hadda Brooks ruined her career by marrying a pimp who beat her, and that troublemakers earn bad reputations.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: The Lyons Brothers bring the Spirits west; the marijuana bust and quitting pot
segments.summary: The Lyons brothers took the Spirits from the Hickory House to Hollywood where all were jailed 45 days over one joint; Bunn quit pot afterward.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Rejected by the draft; bebop musicians dodging; working for Red Callender
segments.summary: He was called, tested and rejected by letter; they discuss bebop musicians feigning craziness, and he worked with bassist Red Callender in L.A. toward the war's end.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Jimmy Bunn the pianist
segments.summary: Pianist Jimmy Bunn and his Japanese wife helped Rosenberg find Bunn; Jimmy kicked a heroin habit while staying with Bunn in San Francisco.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: The importance of family
segments.summary: Bunn says he had few family problems except with his son, and his parents never saw his children.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Cab Calloway and the stolen "Hi-de-ho"
segments.summary: Bunn says Cab Calloway took "hi-de-hi-de-ho" from Leo Watson and the Spirits at a New York after-hours club, and he did not mind.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Rehearsing with Benny Goodman at Mort Davis's rehearsal hall
segments.summary: Preferring small groups, he rehearsed with Benny Goodman before Goodman's big band, was offered a job, but went out on his own.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Hard times in Harlem before leaving in 1942
segments.summary: He fed his group for two months from his night-club earnings, since New York and Harlem were dead before the war.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Musicians, women and jealousy in the group
segments.summary: He says attention from women breeds jealousy in a group, so women should come after work.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Doug's jealousy and why Bunn got out of groups
segments.summary: Doug Daniels was jealous of Bunn's guitar-tossing act, and professional jealousy is why Bunn left groups.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Traditional jazz returning; Papa John Creach
segments.summary: They note veteran players like Hampton and violinist Johnny Creech finding comfortable work again.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Jules Bihari and Modern Records
segments.summary: Bunn describes Jules Bihari as a heavy-drinking man who started by catching acts and built the family record business, with Bunn helping him get into it.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Meeting B.B. King
segments.summary: He met B.B. King in San Francisco and thought him stuck up, but respects that King stuck with the blues.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: What makes the blues powerful: soul and ideas
segments.summary: Bunn says the blues is soul, feeling and above all ideas, and calls a good idea brilliant.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Wrapping up and thanks
segments.summary: Rosenberg asks if Bunn wants to add anything, and Bunn praises him.

segments.chapter: Edgar Hayes, reflections and closing
segments.title: Advice to Rosenberg and finding God in the heart
segments.summary: Bunn urges Rosenberg to keep at his work, and says he found God in his heart and changed his ways when he had a family.
